transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-07-07 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Sally (CTO), Raj (ML Lead), Tom (Infra), Maya (PM)

Summary: quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize - focus on batching and KV/prefix caching cost models. Call end: agreed pilot and docs exchange.

00:00 Lena: hey everyone thanks for joining, should we do quick intros?
00:07 Sally: yeah i'm sally cto at orion payments, thanks for hosting, excited to see how we could reduce inference cost for our chat+payments assistant
00:15 Marco: great, i'm marco, Solutions Engineer, i'll drive the technical piece and run through the cost model and KV cache behavior, there might be a few scribbles in the notes from fireflies so apologies if acronyms get munged
00:26 Raj: raj here, i'm ML lead, our main constraint is 95th pct latency sub 350ms for customer-facing flows, and we want to cut token cost by ~40% if possible
00:38 Priya: quick agenda - current stack, batching basics, KV/prefix cache, cost model example, ops & security Qs, next steps
00:50 Tom: our infra is on aws, using k8s EKS, some inference on sagemaker endpoints for embeddings, and a small self-hosted cluster for sensitive stuff - we do need VPC peering for any private deployment
01:05 Marco: ok cool, so first batching - high level, Redwood continuously batches incoming requests to increase GPU utilization while trying to keep latency SLOs. typical gains depend on request arrival patterns - if you have many short chats you'll see big throughput wins
01:20 Marco: note when i say batching i sometimes shorthand it as 'continuous batching' or 'c-batch' in the docs, sorry if that shows up weird in the transcript
01:28 Raj: does your batching add tail latency? our 95th is tight so we worry about buffering delays
01:33 Marco: yes great q. there's a tradeoff - we tune max batch time and size. for example you can set a max-batch-wait of 10ms and get most of the batching benefit with negligible tail impact; we also do dynamic routing to faster pools to meet SLOs
01:50 Priya: and we have model variants for lower-latency vs low-cost; Redwood can fallback to a smaller quantized variant if the primary is congested
02:03 Sally: ok so batching helps throughput, but our use is bursty during day. what about caching - we've heard prefix cache helps chat a lot
02:13 Marco: absolutely. prefix caching stores prefix kv states so when users ask follow-ups the KV cache avoids recomputing large prefix attention. two modes: prefix (session-level) and KV (key-value cache for embeddings/long context). sometimes the docs use the terms interchangeably which is confusing - sorry about that
02:30 Raj: what's hit rate we can expect? for our use case with payments assistant, users often do a multi-turn session of 5-8 turns, many tokens repeated like masked acc numbers, bank names etc
02:40 Marco: typical hit rates 40-70% depends on prompt design and session length. in our cost model i usually assume conservative 35% for production and optimistic 60% for tuned prompts. that maps to token savings roughly proportional to prefix length.
02:55 Marco: quick example - baseline without cache at 1.0x token cost. with 40% hit rate and prefix re-use we see 0.6-0.7x effective token compute per session. you'll still pay for some KV storage but it's a tiny fraction compared to compute.
03:15 Tom: storage for KV - is that customer data? how's it encrypted?
03:20 Priya: KV gets stored encrypted at rest; for Private deployments you can bring-your-own KMS / HSM. for hosted we offer KMS integration and audit logs. also we rotate keys and provide SOC 2 artifacts.
03:35 Sally: good - we need SOC 2 + SSO (SAML) and audit trail for regulatory review, can you share docs?
03:41 Lena: yes we'll share SOC2 and network diagram plus KMS notes. I'll drop links after the call.
03:48 Raj: curious about cost numbers - can you show a cost model spreadsheet-ish quick?
03:53 Marco: sure, i'll walk through a simplified model: assume 100k sessions/day, avg 500 tokens/session baseline. at $X per 1k tokens (placeholder) baseline compute TCO is X. With batching + KV cache we reduce effective tokens and get throughput improvements so cost drops - in our example we showed ~35-45% cost reduction depending on hit rates and batch sizing.
04:20 Marco: important caveat: batching reduces per-token cost but can increase p99 tail if misconfigured; KV cache reduces compute but needs memory and warmup; there's also quantization tradeoffs which may affect quality.
04:40 Sally: how do you measure quality regression when using quantized models or cache? we cannot degrade fraud detection prompts
04:48 Marco: we pair Optimize with evaluations - you can run prompt sets through both model variants and we track metrics (exact match, rouge, or custom thresholds). Redwood's rollout supports canaries and automatic fallback if quality drops.
05:05 Raj: about private/dedicated - we need VPC peering and bring-your-own KMS for keys. Also would prefer dedicated GPUs for production. what's the minimum commit?
05:16 Lena: for Dedicated we do reserved capacity terms - I'll add contractual slide and pricing to the follow-up. For Private on-prem we have an appliance option but that adds integration work; many customers start Hosted with encryption + VPC and move to Dedicated.
05:30 Tom: network egress - if hosted, do you store logs or kv outside our region? we need data residency in eu-west-1 for some flows
05:38 Priya: we support region pinning and can configure no-cross-region replication for KV. we'll include details in the network doc.
05:45 Maya: one operational quirk - does KV cache cause cold starts when traffic spikes?
05:50 Marco: yes you can see a warmup period; we mitigate with prewarming and predictive caching for sessions that we detect will likely be reused. Also you can tune TTLs to balance memory vs hit rate.
06:05 Marco: quick live sketch of cost model (reading a shared sheet) - baseline numbers are illustrative: 100k sessions, 500 tokens = 50M tokens. cost-per-token compute baseline $0.0002 -> monthly X. With 45% effective token reduction + batching you move to approx $0.00011 per token equivalent.
06:35 Raj: can we run a bench with our exact prompts? we care about p95 and p99 plus cost per 1M requests
06:42 Lena: yes we typically run a 48-hour bench with redwood-optimize config: batch params, kv enabled, model variants. Marco will share the harness.
06:50 Marco: i'll include the harness and a sample dataframe of request arrival distribution, plus instructions to simulate multi-turn sessions for correct prefix keys
07:02 Sally: what about model switching/fallbacks - if you use quantized variant during spikes how do you ensure quality?
07:09 Marco: we use rollout policies - canary to small traffic fraction, and auto-fallback if custom quality monitoring signals a regression. You define guardrails in the console.
07:20 Raj: technical nit - how is KV cache surfaced in APIs? is it automatic or do we manage session ids and keys?
07:27 Priya: session management is app-level but Redwood's SDKs can help manage session ids and prefix keys. for advanced use you can write explicit cache hooks to populate or evict keys. Sometimes the SDK will be mis-read as 'auto-K-V' in notes - it's only helper code.
07:45 Tom: thanks, for compliance we need logs for every request with session id mapping for audits, retention ~12 months. is that possible?
07:54 Priya: yes, long-term retention is an add-on; we can stream logs to your S3 or SIEM.
08:02 Marco: back to cost model - another lever is batching window and adaptive batching. For your bursty daytime pattern we recommend a small max-wait and slightly higher max-batch size to catch micro-bursts without hurting p95. Example config: max_wait 10ms, max_batch 64 for our 8k token model family.
08:25 Raj: can we see actual numbers from similar customers in finance?
08:30 Marco: i can share anonymized case study - we saw 30-50% cost reduction for payments chat workloads with typical hit rates ~45% and batching tuned. i'll pull two examples.
08:40 Sally: ok sounds reasonable. question on billing: is caching billed as separate line item?
08:45 Lena: caching is included as part of Optimize - compute and KV storage are billed separately; storage is minor and compute is main driver. we'll show line items in pricing doc.
08:55 Maya: what about embeddings - do you recommend caching those as well?
09:00 Marco: yes for RAG workflows you can cache embeddings and use nearest-neighbor lookups; KV cache is different - prefix KV is for autoregressive state. Both can reduce compute but with different operational models.
09:15 Raj: one more question on observability - can we get token-level cost breakdown by route and model?
09:20 Priya: yes console has per-route cost and per-model token breakdowns, and you can set alerts on regression.
09:28 Tom: timeline - if we like the bench results we want to pilot in staging in 3 weeks and target production in 8-10 weeks.
09:36 Lena: good, we'll align on pilot scope in follow-up.
09:40 Marco: last note - watch out for prompt formatting; small prompt trims can amplify cache hit rates because fewer unique prefixes; it's a cheap win.
09:52 Sally: perfect thanks, appreciate the walkthrough.
09:56 Lena: recap: we'll send pricing + SOC2 + network + KMS docs, Marco will share benchmark harness and sample configs, customer to share workload distribution and acceptance SLOs. schedule follow-up after benchmark.
10:15 Call ended

Notes on transcript quality: some product names and acronyms might be transcribed oddly (k v cache, c-batch).

References shared: benchmarking spreadsheet (link), SOC2 and network doc (link), sample harness repo (link).
